{"references\codex-tools.md": ["  >   0:## Subagent dispatch requires multi-agent support
  >   1:
  >   2:Add to your Codex config (`~/.codex/config.toml`):
  >   3:
  >   4:```toml
  >   5:[features]
  >   6:multi_agent = true
  >   7:```
  >   8:
  >   9:This enables the multi-agent tools that skills like
  >  10:`dispatching-parallel-agents` and `subagent-driven-development` use.
  >  11:Which tools you get depends on the multi-agent version your model
  >  12:preset selects (current presets run V2; older ones run V1). Trust your
  >  13:actual tool list over any table — including this one — when they
  >  14:disagree.
  >  15:
  >  16:- **Spawning:** give children a clean context with
  >  17:  `spawn_agent {fork_turns: "none"}`; the default `"all"` copies your
  >  18:  entire transcript into the child. On Codex 0.145+, role files under
  >  19:  `~/.codex/agents/` attach to isolated forks via `agent_type`.
  >  20:  Full-history forks accept `model` and `reasoning_effort` overrides
  >  21:  (only `agent_type` is refused there) — isolated forks are the SDD
  >  22:  default for context hygiene, not because overrides require them.
  >  23:- **Fix rounds:** resume the implementer with `followup_task` — it
  >  24:  delivers your message, triggers a turn, and transparently reloads a
  >  25:  child the harness evicted. Never dispatch a fresh implementer on the
  >  26:  theory that a spawned agent cannot be messaged again; on V2 it
  >  27:  always can.
  >  28:- **Lifecycle:** V2 has no `close_agent`. Finished children are
  >  29:  evicted automatically when slots are needed; leaving them unclosed
  >  30:  costs nothing. Only V1 sessions have `close_agent` — there, close
  >  31:  reviewers when their review returns, and close each implementer
  >  32:  after its task's review passes.
  >  33:- **Model names:** never copy a model name from a skill, table, or old
  >  34:  session into `spawn_agent` without checking it against your current
  >  35:  spawn allowlist — V2 accepts only V2-capable presets and hard-errors
  >  36:  on the rest.
  >  37:
  >  38:## Waiting on children
  >  39:
  >  40:`wait_agent` is an event subscription, not a poll: a long wait wakes
  >  41:the moment a child produces mailbox activity, with the same latency as
  >  42:a short one. Short-timeout polling buys nothing and costs a tool call —
  >  43:and a context rebill — per poll. In measured sessions, roughly
  >  44:two-thirds of all wait calls were short polls that timed out.
  >  45:
  >  46:- While you still have local work, do not wait at all. A completed
  >  47:  child's final answer is pushed into your mailbox and arrives with
  >  48:  your next turn.
  >  49:- When you are genuinely idle with children outstanding, wait in
  >  50:  bounded stretches: `wait_agent` with `timeout_ms` 300000-600000
  >  51:  (5-10 minutes). After each stretch — wake or timeout — post one
  >  52:  status line, run `list_agents`, and chase any child that finished
  >  53:  without reporting. Never stack polls shorter than five minutes; the
  >  54:  event subscription wakes a bounded stretch just as fast as a short
  >  55:  one.
  >  56:- Completion mail cannot wake an idle controller (it is delivered
  >  57:  without triggering a turn); covering that idle window is
  >  58:  `wait_agent`'s only job. A stretch that times out with no activity
  >  59:  is your cue to reconcile, not to shorten the next stretch.
  >  60:
  >  61:## Model routing on spawns
  >  62:
  >  63:Every `spawn_agent` you issue — including when you are yourself a
  >  64:spawned child running a fan-out — sets `model` AND `reasoning_effort`
  >  65:explicitly, per the Model Selection rules of the skill you are
  >  66:executing. Setting `model` alone is a trap: the child's effort
  >  67:silently resets to that model's default, not to yours.

  >  70:`~/.codex/config.toml` so any spawn that slips through still routes to

  >  75:[agents]
  >  76:default_subagent_model = "<a mid-tier model from your spawn allowlist>"
  >  77:default_subagent_reasoning_effort = "medium"
  >  78:```

  >  84:

  >  87:GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)

  >   1:name: systematic-debugging
  >   2:description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
  >   3:---
  >   4:
  >   5:# Systematic Debugging
  >   6:
  >   7:## Overview
  >   8:
  >   9:**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.
  >  10:
  >  11:**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**
  >  12:
  >  13:## The Iron Law
  >  14:
  >  15:```
  >  16:NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
  >  17:```
  >  18:
  >  19:If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.
  >  20:
  >  21:## When to Use
  >  22:
  >  23:Use for ANY technical issue:
  >  24:- Test failures
  >  25:- Bugs in production
  >  26:- Unexpected behavior
  >  27:- Performance problems
  >  28:- Build failures
  >  29:- Integration issues
  >  30:
  >  31:**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
  >  32:- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
  >  33:- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
  >  34:- You've already tried multiple fixes
  >  35:- Previous fix didn't work
  >  36:- You don't fully understand the issue
  >  37:
  >  38:**Don't skip when:**
  >  39:- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
  >  40:- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
  >  41:- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)
  >  42:
  >  43:## The Four Phases
  >  44:
  >  45:You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
  >  46:
  >  47:### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation
  >  48:
  >  49:**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**
  >  50:
  >  51:1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
  >  52:   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
  >  53:   - They often contain the exact solution
  >  54:   - Read stack traces completely
  >  55:   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes
  >  56:
  >  57:2. **Reproduce Consistently**
  >  58:   - Can you trigger it reliably?
  >  59:   - What are the exact steps?
  >  60:   - Does it happen every time?
  >  61:   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess
  >  62:
  >  63:3. **Check Recent Changes**
  >  64:   - What changed that could cause this?
  >  65:   - Git diff, recent commits
  >  66:   - New dependencies, config changes
  >  67:   - Environmental differences
  >  68:
  >  69:4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**
  >  70:
  >  71:   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**
  >  72:
  >  73:   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
  >  74:   ```
  >  75:   For EACH component boundary:
  >  76:     - Log what data enters component
  >  77:     - Log what data exits component
  >  78:     - Verify environment/config propagation
  >  79:     - Check state at each layer
  >  80:
  >  81:   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
  >  82:   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
  >  83:   THEN investigate that specific component
  >  84:   ```
  >  85:
  >  86:   **Example (multi-layer system):**
  >  87:   ```bash
  >  88:   # Layer 1: Workflow
  >  89:   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
  >  90:   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"
  >  91:
  >  92:   # Layer 2: Build script
  >  93:   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
  >  94:   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"
  >  95:
  >  96:   # Layer 3: Signing script
  >  97:   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
  >  98:   security list-keychains
  >  99:   security find-identity -v
  > 100:
  > 101:   # Layer 4: Actual signing
  > 102:   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
  > 103:   ```
  > 104:
  > 105:   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)
  > 106:
  > 107:5. **Trace Data Flow**
  > 108:
  > 109:   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**
  > 110:
  > 111:   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.
  > 112:
  > 113:   **Quick version:**
  > 114:   - Where does bad value originate?
  > 115:   - What called this with bad value?
  > 116:   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
  > 117:   - Fix at source, not at symptom
  > 118:
  > 119:### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis
  > 120:
  > 121:**Find the pattern before fixing:**
  > 122:
  > 123:1. **Find Working Examples**
  > 124:   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
  > 125:   - What works that's similar to what's broken?
  > 126:
  > 127:2. **Compare Against References**
  > 128:   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
  > 129:   - Don't skim - read every line
  > 130:   - Understand the pattern fully before applying
  > 131:
  > 132:3. **Identify Differences**
  > 133:   - What's different between working and broken?
  > 134:   - List every difference, however small
  > 135:   - Don't assume "that can't matter"
  > 136:
  > 137:4. **Understand Dependencies**
  > 138:   - What other components does this need?
  > 139:   - What settings, config, environment?
  > 140:   - What assumptions does it make?
  > 141:
  > 142:### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing
  > 143:
  > 144:**Scientific method:**
  > 145:
  > 146:1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
  > 147:   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
  > 148:   - Write it down
  > 149:   - Be specific, not vague
  > 150:
  > 151:2. **Test Minimally**
  > 152:   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
  > 153:   - One variable at a time
  > 154:   - Don't fix multiple things at once
  > 155:
  > 156:3. **Verify Before Continuing**
  > 157:   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
  > 158:   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
  > 159:   - DON'T add more fixes on top
  > 160:
  > 161:4. **When You Don't Know**
  > 162:   - Say "I don't understand X"
  > 163:   - Don't pretend to know
  > 164:   - Ask for help
  > 165:   - Research more
  > 166:
  > 167:### Phase 4: Implementation
  > 168:
  > 169:**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**
  > 170:
  > 171:1. **Create Failing Test Case**
  > 172:   - Simplest possible reproduction
  > 173:   - Automated test if possible
  > 174:   - One-off test script if no framework
  > 175:   - MUST have before fixing
  > 176:   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests
  > 177:
  > 178:2. **Implement Single Fix**
  > 179:   - Address the root cause identified
  > 180:   - ONE change at a time
  > 181:   - No "while I'm here" improvements
  > 182:   - No bundled refactoring
  > 183:
  > 184:3. **Verify Fix**
  > 185:   - Test passes now?
  > 186:   - No other tests broken?
  > 187:   - Issue actually resolved?
  > 188:   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success
  > 189:
  > 190:4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
  > 191:   - STOP
  > 192:   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
  > 193:   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
  > 194:   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
  > 195:   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion
  > 196:
  > 197:5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**
  > 198:
  > 199:   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
  > 200:   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
  > 201:   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
  > 202:   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere
  > 203:
  > 204:   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
  > 205:   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
  > 206:   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
  > 207:   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?
  > 208:
  > 209:   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**
  > 210:
  > 211:   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.
  > 212:
  > 213:## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process
  > 214:
  > 215:If you catch yourself thinking:
  > 216:- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
  > 217:- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
  > 218:- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
  > 219:- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
  > 220:- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
  > 221:- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
  > 222:- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
  > 223:- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
  > 224:- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
  > 225:- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
  > 226:- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**
  > 227:
  > 228:**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**
  > 229:
  > 230:**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)
  > 231:
  > 232:## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong
  > 233:
  > 234:**Watch for these redirections:**
  > 235:- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
  > 236:- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
  > 237:- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
  > 238:- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
  > 239:- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working
  > 240:
  > 241:**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.
  > 242:
  > 243:## Common Rationalizations
  > 244:
  > 245:| Excuse | Reality |
  > 246:|--------|---------|
  > 247:| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
  > 248:| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
  > 249:| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
  > 250:| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
  > 251:| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
  > 252:| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
  > 253:| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
  > 254:| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |
  > 255:
  > 256:## Quick Reference
  > 257:
  > 258:| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
  > 259:|-------|---------------|------------------|
  > 260:| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
  > 261:| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
  > 262:| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
  > 263:| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |
  > 264:
  > 265:## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"
  > 266:
  > 267:If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:
  > 268:
  > 269:1. You've completed the process
  > 270:2. Document what you investigated
  > 271:3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
  > 272:4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation
  > 273:
  > 274:**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.
  > 275:
  > 276:## Supporting Techniques
  > 277:
  > 278:These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:
  > 279:
  > 280:- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
  > 281:- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
  > 282:- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling"]}

  > 238:- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms

  > 240:

  > 242:

  > 246:|--------|---------|

  > 248:| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |

  > 262:| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
  > 263:| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

  > 268:

  > 270:2. Document what you investigated
  > 271:3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
  > 272:4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation
  > 273:

  > 275:

  > 277:

  > 235:| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

  > 244:- Rationalizing "just this once"

  > 246:- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
  > 247:- "It's about spirit not ritual"

  > 249:- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
  > 250:- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
  > 251:- "This is different because..."

  > 287:```

  > 291:

  > 298:- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
  > 299:- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test

  > 301:- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
  > 302:- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
  > 303:- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

  > 310:|---------|----------|
  > 311:| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |

  > 313:| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |

  > 316:## Debugging Integration
  > 317:
  > 318:Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

  > 324:```
  > 325:Production code → test exists and failed first
  > 326:Otherwise → not TDD
  > 327:```
  > 328:
  > 329:No exceptions without your human partner's permission."]}

  > 129:Expected: PASS
  > 130:

  > 132:

  > 134:git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
  > 135:git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
  > 136:```
  > 137:````
  > 138:

  > 140:
  > 141:A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
  > 142:from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
  > 143:of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:
  > 144:
  > 145:- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  > 146:  spec's exact values in them.
  > 147:- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  > 148:  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  > 149:  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  > 150:  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
  > 151:- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  > 152:  passed.
  > 153:- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  > 154:  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.
  > 155:
  > 156:A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
  > 157:longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
  > 158:decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
  > 159:"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
  > 160:opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.
  > 161:
  > 162:## Self-Review
  > 163:
  > 164:After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.
  > 165:
  > 166:**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.
  > 167:
  > 168:**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.
  > 169:
  > 170:**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.
  > 171:
  > 172:**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it?   >   3:---
  >   4:
  >   5:# Verification Before Completion
  >   6:
  >   7:## Overview
  >   8:
  >   9:**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.
  >  10:
  >  11:**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**
  >  12:
  >  13:## The Iron Law
  >  14:
  >  15:```
  >  16:NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
  >  17:```
  >  18:
  >  19:If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.
  >  20:
  >  21:## The Gate Function
  >  22:
  >  23:```
  >  24:BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:
  >  25:
  >  26:1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
  >  27:2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
  >  28:3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
  >  29:4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
  >  30:   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
  >  31:   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
  >  32:5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim
  >  33:
  >  34:Skip any step = lying, not verifying
  >  35:```
  >  36:
  >  37:## Common Failures
  >  38:
  >  39:| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
  >  40:|-------|----------|----------------|
  >  41:| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
  >  42:| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
  >  43:| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
  >  44:| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
  >  45:| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
  >  46:| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
  >  47:| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |
  >  48:
  >  49:## Red Flags - STOP
  >  50:
  >  51:- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
  >  52:- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
  >  53:- About to commit/push/PR without verification
  >  54:- Trusting agent success reports
  >  55:- Relying on partial verification
  >  56:- Thinking "just this once"
  >  57:- Tired and wanting work over
  >  58:- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**
  >  59:
  >  60:## Rationalization Prevention
  >  61:
  >  62:| Excuse | Reality |
  >  63:|--------|---------|
  >  64:| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
  >  65:| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
  >  66:| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
  >  67:| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
  >  68:| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
  >  69:| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
  >  70:| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
  >  71:| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |
  >  72:
  >  73:## Key Patterns
  >  74:
  >  75:**Tests:**
  >  76:```
  >  77:✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
  >  78:❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
  >  79:```
  >  80:
  >  81:**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
  >  82:```
  >  83:✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
  >  84:❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
  >  85:```
  >  86:
  >  87:**Build:**
  >  88:```
  >  89:✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
  >  90:❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
  >  91:```
  >  92:
  >  93:**Requirements:**
  >  94:```
  >  95:✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
  >  96:❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
  >  97:```
  >  98:
  >  99:**Agent delegation:**
  > 100:```
  > 101:✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
  > 102:❌ Trust agent report
  > 103:```
  > 104:
  > 105:## When To Apply
  > 106:
  > 107:**ALWAYS before:**
  > 108:- ANY variation of success/completion claims
  > 109:- ANY expression of satisfaction
  > 110:- ANY positive statement about work state
  > 111:- Committing, PR creation, task completion
  > 112:- Moving to next task
  > 113:- Delegating to agents
  > 114:
  > 115:**Rule applies to:**
  > 116:- Exact phrases
  > 117:- Paraphrases and synonyms
  > 118:- Implications of success
  > 119:- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness"]}

{"test-driven-development\writing-good-tests.md": ["  >   0:# Writing Good Tests
  >   1:
  >   2:**Load this reference when:** writing or changing tests, adding mocks, or
  >   3:adding cleanup/helper methods for tests.
  >   4:
  >   5:## Overview
  >   6:
  >   7:A test exists to catch a specific break. Two principles govern everything
  >   8:here:
  >   9:
  >  10:```
  >  11:1. Every test names the break it catches
  >  12:2. Every test exercises the real thing
  >  13:```
  >  14:
  >  15:Strict TDD produces both naturally: a test written first and watched
  >  16:failing against real code has already proven it can fail, and only earns
  >  17:a mock when the real dependency proves slow or external.
  >  18:
  >  19:## Principle 1: Name the Break
  >  20:
  >  21:Before writing the test body, answer: **what production change should
  >  22:make this test fail — and is that change a bug or a decision?** A test
  >  23:earns its place by catching a wrong branch, missing side effect, wrong
  >  24:argument, boundary case, or broken contract.
  >  25:
  >  26:**Derive expectations independently.** Use literals and hand-checked
  >  27:fixtures; table-driven tests with literal `want` values are the preferred
  >  28:shape. An expectation computed by the code under test — or its helpers —
  >  29:passes no matter what that code does:
  >  30:
  >  31:```typescript
  >  32:// ❌ Mirror assertion: the same builder computes both sides — always true
  >  33:const expected = buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' });
  >  34:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe(expected);
  >  35:
  >  36:// ✅ Hand-derived literal
  >  37:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe('tag:"urgent"');
  >  38:```
  >  39:
  >  40:**No change detectors.** If only intentional decisions can fail a test —
  >  41:a constant's value, exact message wording, private structure — it fires
  >  42:on redesign and sleeps through bugs. Test the behavior that depends on
  >  43:the decision: not `expect(MAX_RETRIES).toBe(5)` but "a failing call is
  >  44:retried 5 times and the 6th attempt never happens."
  >  45:
  >  46:**Behavior, not text.** Asserting that a script, skill, or config
  >  47:contains an exact line proves only that the source is the source. Run
  >  48:scripts against controlled inputs and assert outputs, side effects, or
  >  49:exit codes. Documents that instruct agents are tested by the consuming
  >  50:agent's behavior (superpowers:writing-skills); prose for humans earns no
  >  51:test at all.
  >  52:
  >  53:**Your code, not the framework.** Test the contract your code makes at
  >  54:its boundaries — the route you register, the query you emit, the payload
  >  55:you produce. Upstream mechanics are their maintainers' tests to write
  >  56:(the classic: asserting your router invokes a registered handler — that
  >  57:is the framework's test, not yours). When upstream behavior genuinely
  >  58:surprised you, write one narrow characterization test naming the
  >  59:assumption. The same boundary applies inside your code: constructors,
  >  60:getters, constants, and trivial forwarding earn tests only when they
  >  61:validate, normalize, default, derive, enforce, or cause side effects —
  >  62:otherwise assert the first consumer-visible result that depends on them.
  >  63:
  >  64:### Gate Function
  >  65:
  >  66:```
  >  67:BEFORE writing the test body:
  >  68:  Name the production change that would make this test fail.
  >  69:
  >  70:  Cannot name one            → redesign around an observable behavior
  >  71:  "The source text changed"  → run the artifact and assert its effects
  >  72:  Only intentional decisions → change detector; test the behavior
  >  73:                               that depends on the decision
  >  74:
  >  75:  Confirm the expected value is derived without the code under test.
  >  76:  IF it reuses the code's logic or helpers:
  >  77:    Replace it with a literal or hand-checked fixture
  >  78:```
  >  79:
  >  80:## Principle 2: Exercise the Real Thing
  >  81:
  >  82:**The mock earns no assertions.** A mock assertion passes when the mock
  >  83:is present and fails when it is absent — it says nothing about the
  >  84:component. Assert the real component's behavior; if the mock is what you
  >  85:are checking, unmock it or delete the assertion.
  >  86:
  >  87:```typescript
  >  88:// ✅ Real behavior
  >  89:expect(screen.getByRole('navigation')).toBeInTheDocument();
  >  90:
  >  91:// ❌ Mock existence
  >  92:expect(screen.getByTestId('sidebar-mock')).toBeInTheDocument();
  >  93:```
  >  94:
  >  95:**your human partner's correction:** "Are we testing the behavior of a
  >  96:mock?"
  >  97:
  >  98:**Mock at the right level.** Learn every side effect of the real method
  >  99:before replacing it; mock the slow or external operation and keep what
  > 100:the test depends on real. When unsure, run the test against the real
  > 101:implementation first and observe what actually needs to happen.
  > 102:
  > 103:```typescript
  > 104:// ❌ The mock swallows the config write that duplicate detection reads
  > 105:vi.mock('ToolCatalog', () => ({
  > 106:  discoverAndCacheTools: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  > 107:}));
  > 108:
  > 109:// ✅ Mock only the slow server startup; the config write stays real
  > 110:vi.mock('MCPServerManager');
  > 111:```
  > 112:
  > 113:**Make doubles specific.** When arguments, call counts, or ordering are
  > 114:part of the contract, assert them — a fake that accepts anything verifies
  > 115:nothing. Give each branch (success, error, malformed) its own fixture or
  > 116:spy, so the wrong branch cannot satisfy the expectation.
  > 117:
  > 118:**Mirror real data completely.** Mock the complete structure as it exists
  > 119:in reality — all documented fields — not just the ones your test reads.
  > 120:Partial mocks fail silently when downstream code reads an omitted field:
  > 121:the test passes while integration breaks.
  > 122:
  > 123:**Production classes carry production methods only.** Cleanup that only
  > 124:tests need lives in test utilities, never as a `destroy()` on the
  > 125:production class. Ask: is this method called only from tests? Does this
  > 126:class own this resource's lifecycle? Wrong answers → test utility.
  > 127:
  > 128:**Prefer real components over complex mocks.** When mock setup outgrows
  > 129:the test logic, mocks miss methods the real components have, or tests
  > 130:break when the mock changes, switch to an integration test with real
  > 131:components. **your human partner's question:** "Do we need to be using a
  > 132:mock here?"
  > 133:
  > 134:### Gate Function
  > 135:
  > 136:```
  > 137:BEFORE adding a mock or test helper:
  > 138:  List the real method's side effects; keep the ones the test
  > 139:  depends on real — mock the slow/external level below them.
  > 140:
  > 141:  Mock responses mirror the complete real structure.
  > 142:
  > 143:  A method only tests call lives in test utilities, not production.
  > 144:
  > 145:  About to assert on the mock itself?
  > 146:    Unmock it or delete the assertion.
  > 147:```
  > 148:
  > 149:## Tests Ship With the Implementation
  > 150:
  > 151:The TDD cycle — failing test, minimal implementation, refactor — is what
  > 152:"complete" means. Ship the tests the behavior needs and only those:
  > 153:trivial code and human prose earn none, and a test written to satisfy
  > 154:process costs maintenance forever.
  > 155:
  > 156:## The Mutation Check
  > 157:
  > 158:Before finishing, mentally mutate the production code; at least one test
  > 159:should fail for each realistic mutation:
  > 160:
  > 161:- Wrong constant or argument
  > 162:- Wrong branch handler
  > 163:- Missing state change or side effect
  > 164:- Empty or default return
  > 165:- Missing validation for zero, empty, nil, unauthorized, or malformed input
  > 166:
  > 167:A mutation nothing catches marks the behavior as unprotected — or the
  > 168:test as tautological.
  > 169:
  > 170:## Quick Reference
  > 171:
  > 172:| When you... | Do |
  > 173:|-------------|-----|
  > 174:| Write any test | Name the break it catches — a bug, not a decision |
  > 175:| Build an expected value | Derive it by hand; never with the code under test |
  > 176:| Test a script or document | Run it / pressure-test its consumer; never grep its text |
  > 177:| Reach for a dependency test | Test your boundary contract, not their documented mechanics |
  > 178:| Want to assert on a mocked element | Test the real component, or unmock it |
  > 179:| Are about to mock a method | Learn its side effects; mock the slow/external level |
  > 180:| Build a mock response | Mirror the real structure completely |
  > 181:| Need cleanup only tests use | Put it in test utilities |
  > 182:| Watch mock setup balloon | Switch to an integration test with real components |
  > 183:| Finish a test file | Run the mutation check |
  > 184:
  > 185:## Warning Signs
  > 186:
  > 187:- Setup and assertion share the same object, guaranteeing equality
  > 188:- The test can fail only through a panic, crash, or missing selector
  > 189:- The test fails on every intentional change, never on accidental breakage
  > 190:- Expected values are hidden behind loops, builders, or helpers
  > 191:- The test greps source text, or asserts a removed symbol stays removed
  > 192:- The test would still matter if only the framework remained
  > 193:- The test exists for coverage, checking no side effect or outcome
  > 194:- An assertion checks a `*-mock` test ID, or fails if you remove the mock
  > 195:- A method is called only from test files
  > 196:- Mock setup is more than half the test, or you can't explain why the mock is needed
  > 197:- Mocking "just to be safe""]}

  >  21:Before writing the test body, answer: **what production change should
  >  22:make this test fail — and is that change a bug or a decision?** A test
  >  23:earns its place by catching a wrong branch, missing side effect, wrong
  >  24:argument, boundary case, or broken contract.
  >  25:
  >  26:**Derive expectations independently.** Use literals and hand-checked
  >  27:fixtures; table-driven tests with literal `want` values are the preferred
  >  28:shape. An expectation computed by the code under test — or its helpers —
  >  29:passes no matter what that code does:
  >  30:
  >  31:```typescript
  >  32:// ❌ Mirror assertion: the same builder computes both sides — always true
  >  33:const expected = buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' });
  >  34:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe(expected);
  >  35:
  >  36:// ✅ Hand-derived literal
  >  37:expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe('tag:"urgent"');
  >  38:```
  >  39:
  >  40:**No change detectors.** If only intentional decisions can fail a test —
  >  41:a constant's value, exact message wording, private structure — it fires
  >  42:on redesign and sleeps through bugs. Test the behavior that depends on
  >  43:the decision: not `expect(MAX_RETRIES).toBe(5)` but "a failing call is
  >  44:retried 5 times and the 6th attempt never happens."
  >  45:
  >  46:**Behavior, not text.** Asserting that a script, skill, or config
  >  47:contains an exact line proves only that the source is the source. Run
  >  48:scripts against controlled inputs and assert outputs, side effects, or
  >  49:exit codes. Documents that instruct agents are tested by the consuming
  >  50:agent's behavior (superpowers:writing-skills); prose for humans earns no
  >  51:test at all.
  >  52:
  >  53:**Your code, not the framework.** Test the contract your code makes at
  >  54:its boundaries — the route you register, the query you emit, the payload
  >  55:you produce. Upstream mechanics are their maintainers' tests to write
  >  56:(the classic: asserting your router invokes a registered handler — that
  >  57:is the framework's test, not yours). When upstream behavior genuinely
  >  58:surprised you, write one narrow characterization test naming the
  >  59:assumption. The same boundary applies inside your code: constructors,
  >  60:getters, constants, and trivial forwarding earn tests only when they
  >  61:validate, normalize, default, derive, enforce, or cause side effects —
  >  62:otherwise assert the first consumer-visible result that depends on them.

  >  65:

  >  73:                               that depends on the decision
  >  74:

  >  76:  IF it reuses the code's logic or helpers:

  >  78:```

  >  83:is present and fails when it is absent — it says nothing about the
  >  84:component. Assert the real component's behavior; if the mock is what you
  >  85:are checking, unmock it or delete the assertion.

  >  88:// ✅ Real behavior
  >  89:expect(screen.getByRole('navigation')).toBeInTheDocument();
  >  90:
  >  91:// ❌ Mock existence

  >  93:```
  >  94:

  >  96:mock?"
  >  97:
  >  98:**Mock at the right level.** Learn every side effect of the real method
  >  99:before replacing it; mock the slow or external operation and keep what
  > 100:the test depends on real. When unsure, run the test against the real
  > 101:implementation first and observe what actually needs to happen.
  > 102:
  > 103:```typescript
  > 104:// ❌ The mock swallows the config write that duplicate detection reads
  > 105:vi.mock('ToolCatalog', () => ({
  > 106:  discoverAndCacheTools: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
  > 107:}));
  > 108:

  > 110:vi.mock('MCPServerManager');
  > 111:```

  > 114:part of the contract, assert them — a fake that accepts anything verifies
  > 115:nothing. Give each branch (success, error, malformed) its own fixture or
  > 116:spy, so the wrong branch cannot satisfy the expectation.
  > 117:
  > 118:**Mirror real data completely.** Mock the complete structure as it exists
  > 119:in reality — all documented fields — not just the ones your test reads.
  > 120:Partial mocks fail silently when downstream code reads an omitted field:
  > 121:the test passes while integration breaks.
  > 122:
  > 123:**Production classes carry production methods only.** Cleanup that only
  > 124:tests need lives in test utilities, never as a `destroy()` on the
  > 125:production class. Ask: is this method called only from tests? Does this
  > 126:class own this resource's lifecycle? Wrong answers → test utility.
  > 127:

  > 129:the test logic, mocks miss methods the real components have, or tests
  > 130:break when the mock changes, switch to an integration test with real
  > 131:components. **your human partner's question:** "Do we need to be using a
  > 132:mock here?"
  > 133:

  > 135:
  > 136:```
  > 137:BEFORE adding a mock or test helper:
  > 138:  List the real method's side effects; keep the ones the test
  > 139:  depends on real — mock the slow/external level below them.
  > 140:
  > 141:  Mock responses mirror the complete real structure.
  > 142:
  > 143:  A method only tests call lives in test utilities, not production.
  > 144:

  > 146:    Unmock it or delete the assertion.
  > 147:```

  > 152:"complete" means. Ship the tests the behavior needs and only those:
  > 153:trivial code and human prose earn none, and a test written to satisfy
  > 154:process costs maintenance forever.
  > 155:

  > 157:

  > 159:should fail for each realistic mutation:

  > 162:- Wrong branch handler
  > 163:- Missing state change or side effect

  > 168:test as tautological.
  > 169:

  > 171:
  > 172:| When you... | Do |
  > 173:|-------------|-----|
  > 174:| Write any test | Name the break it catches — a bug, not a decision |
  > 175:| Build an expected value | Derive it by hand; never with the code under test |
  > 176:| Test a script or document | Run it / pressure-test its consumer; never grep its text |
  > 177:| Reach for a dependency test | Test your boundary contract, not their documented mechanics |
  > 178:| Want to assert on a mocked element | Test the real component, or unmock it |
  > 179:| Are about to mock a method | Learn its side effects; mock the slow/external level |
  > 180:| Build a mock response | Mirror the real structure completely |
  > 181:| Need cleanup only tests use | Put it in test utilities |
  > 182:| Watch mock setup balloon | Switch to an integration test with real components |
  > 183:| Finish a test file | Run the mutation check |
  > 184:

  > 186:
  > 187:- Setup and assertion share the same object, guaranteeing equality
  > 188:- The test can fail only through a panic, crash, or missing selector
  > 189:- The test fails on every intentional change, never on accidental breakage
  > 190:- Expected values are hidden behind loops, builders, or helpers
  > 191:- The test greps source text, or asserts a removed symbol stays removed
  > 192:- The test would still matter if only the framework remained
  > 193:- The test exists for coverage, checking no side effect or outcome
  > 194:- An assertion checks a `*-mock` test ID, or fails if you remove the mock
  > 195:- A method is called only from test files
  > 196:- Mock setup is more than half the test, or you can't explain why the mock is needed
  > 197:- Mocking "just to be safe""]}

{"systematic-debugging\root-cause-tracing.md": ["  >   0:# Root Cause Tracing
  >   1:
  >   2:## Overview
  >   3:
  >   4:Bugs often manifest deep in the call stack (git init in wrong directory, file created in wrong location, database opened with wrong path). Your instinct is to fix where the error appears, but that's treating a symptom.
  >   5:
  >   6:**Core principle:** Trace backward through the call chain until you find the original trigger, then fix at the source.
  >   7:
  >   8:## When to Use
  >   9:
  >  10:```dot
  >  11:digraph when_to_use {
  >  12:    "Bug appears deep in stack?" [shape=diamond];
  >  13:    "Can trace backwards?" [shape=diamond];
  >  14:    "Fix at symptom point" [shape=box];
  >  15:    "Trace to original trigger" [shape=box];
  >  16:    "BETTER: Also add defense-in-depth" [shape=box];
  >  17:
  >  18:    "Bug appears deep in stack?" -> "Can trace backwards?" [label="yes"];
  >  19:    "Can trace backwards?" -> "Trace to original trigger" [label="yes"];
  >  20:    "Can trace backwards?" -> "Fix at symptom point" [label="no - dead end"];
  >  21:    "Trace to original trigger" -> "BETTER: Also add defense-in-depth";
  >  22:}
  >  23:```
  >  24:
  >  25:**Use when:**
  >  26:- Error happens deep in execution (not at entry point)
  >  27:- Stack trace shows long call chain
  >  28:- Unclear where invalid data originated
  >  29:- Need to find which test/code triggers the problem
  >  30:
  >  31:## The Tracing Process
  >  32:
  >  33:### 1. Observe the Symptom
  >  34:```
  >  35:Error: git init failed in ~/project/packages/core
  >  36:```
  >  37:
  >  38:### 2. Find Immediate Cause
  >  39:**What code directly causes this?**
  >  40:```typescript
  >  41:await execFileAsync('git', ['init'], { cwd: projectDir });
  >  42:```
  >  43:
  >  44:### 3. Ask: What Called This?
  >  45:```typescript
  >  46:WorktreeManager.createSessionWorktree(projectDir, sessionId)
  >  47:  → called by Session.initializeWorkspace()
  >  48:  → called by Session.create()
  >  49:  → called by test at Project.create()
  >  50:```
  >  51:
  >  52:### 4. Keep Tracing Up
  >  53:**What value was passed?**
  >  54:- `projectDir = ''` (empty string!)
  >  55:- Empty string as `cwd` resolves to `process.cwd()`
  >  56:- That's the source code directory!
  >  57:
  >  58:### 5. Find Original Trigger
  >  59:**Where did empty string come from?**
  >  60:```typescript
  >  61:const context = setupCoreTest(); // Returns { tempDir: '' }
  >  62:Project.create('name', context.tempDir); // Accessed before beforeEach!
  >  63:```
  >  64:
  >  65:## Adding Stack Traces
  >  66:
  >  67:When you can't trace manually, add instrumentation:
  >  68:
  >  69:```typescript
  >  70:// Before the problematic operation
  >  71:async function gitInit(directory: string) {
  >  72:  const stack = new Error().stack;
  >  73:  console.error('DEBUG git init:', {
  >  74:    directory,
  >  75:    cwd: process.cwd(),
  >  76:    nodeEnv: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  >  77:    stack,
  >  78:  });
  >  79:
  >  80:  await execFileAsync('git', ['init'], { cwd: directory });
  >  81:}
  >  82:```
  >  83:
  >  84:**Critical:** Use `console.error()` in tests (not logger - may not show)
  >  85:
  >  86:**Run and capture:**
  >  87:```bash
  >  88:npm test 2>&1 | grep 'DEBUG git init'
  >  89:```
  >  90:
  >  91:**Analyze stack traces:**
  >  92:- Look for test file names
  >  93:- Find the line number triggering the call
  >  94:- Identify the pattern (same test? same parameter?)
  >  95:
  >  96:## Finding Which Test Causes Pollution
  >  97:
  >  98:If something appears during tests but you don't know which test:
  >  99:
  > 100:Use the bisection script `find-polluter.sh` in this directory:
  > 101:
  > 102:```bash
  > 103:bash ./find-polluter.sh '.git' 'src/**/*.test.ts'
  > 104:```
  > 105:
  > 106:Runs tests one-by-one, stops at first polluter. See script for usage.
  > 107:
  > 108:## Real Example: Empty projectDir
  > 109:
  > 110:**Symptom:** `.git` created in `packages/core/` (source code)
  > 111:
  > 112:**Trace chain:**
  > 113:1. `git init` runs in `process.cwd()` ← empty cwd parameter
  > 114:2. WorktreeManager called with empty projectDir
  > 115:3. Session.create() passed empty string
  > 116:4. Test accessed `context.tempDir` before beforeEach
  > 117:5. setupCoreTest() returns `{ tempDir: '' }` initially
  > 118:
  > 119:**Root cause:** Top-level variable initialization accessing empty value
  > 120:
  > 121:**Fix:** Made tempDir a getter that throws if accessed before beforeEach
  > 122:
  > 123:**Also added defense-in-depth:**
  > 124:- Layer 1: Project.create() validates directory
  > 125:- Layer 2: WorkspaceManager validates not empty
  > 126:- Layer 3: NODE_ENV guard refuses git init outside tmpdir
  > 127:- Layer 4: Stack trace logging before git init
  > 128:
  > 129:## Key Principle
  > 130:
  > 131:```dot
  > 132:digraph principle {
  > 133:    "Found immediate cause" [shape=ellipse];
  > 134:    "Can trace one level up?" [shape=diamond];
  > 135:    "Trace backwards" [shape=box];
  > 136:    "Is this the source?" [shape=diamond];
  > 137:    "Fix at source" [shape=box];
  > 138:    "Add validation at each layer" [shape=box];
  > 139:    "Bug impossible" [shape=doublecircle];
  > 140:    "NEVER fix just the symptom" [shape=octagon, style=filled, fillcolor=red, fontcolor=white];
  > 141:
  > 142:    "Found immediate cause" -> "Can trace one level up?";
  > 143:    "Can trace one level up?" -> "Trace backwards" [label="yes"];
  > 144:    "Can trace one level up?" -> "NEVER fix just the symptom" [label="no"];
  > 145:    "Trace backwards" -> "Is this the source?";
  > 146:    "Is this the source?" -> "Trace backwards" [label="no - keeps going"];
  > 147:    "Is this the source?" -> "Fix at source" [label="yes"];
  > 148:    "Fix at source" -> "Add validation at each layer";
  > 149:    "Add validation at each layer" -> "Bug impossible";
  > 150:}
  > 151:```
  > 152:
  > 153:**NEVER fix just where the error appears.** Trace back to find the original trigger.
  > 154:
  > 155:## Stack Trace Tips
  > 156:
  > 157:**In tests:** Use `console.error()` not logger - logger may be suppressed
  > 158:**Before operation:** Log before the dangerous operation, not after it fails
  > 159:**Include context:** Directory, cwd, environment variables, timestamps
  > 160:**Capture stack:** `new Error().stack` shows complete call chain
  > 161:
  > 162:## Real-World Impact
  > 163:
  > 164:From debugging session (2025-10-03):
  > 165:- Found root cause through 5-level trace
  > 166:- Fixed at source (getter validation)
  > 167:- Added 4 layers of defense
  > 168:- 1847 tests passed, zero pollution"]}

  >   1:name: executing-plans
  >   2:description: Use when executing an implementation plan in the current session as the implementer yourself — your human partner chose inline execution, or no subagent tool is available
  >   3:---
  >   4:
  >   5:# Executing Plans
  >   6:
  >   7:Execute the plan yourself, task by task, in this session: no implementer
  >   8:subagent per task, no reviewer per task. One fresh-context review of the
  >   9:whole branch at the end.
  >  10:
  >  11:**Why inline:** Subagent-driven development pays for a fresh implementer
  >  12:and a fresh reviewer on every task, each re-reading the codebase from zero.
  >  13:Inline execution pays for one context (yours) plus one reviewer at the end.
  >  14:What it gives up is a fresh context per task and a second pair of eyes per
  >  15:task. This skill keeps what those two things bought, by other means: the
  >  16:brief is the spec, the ledger is your memory, TDD is the per-task gate, and
  >  17:the final reviewer is the second pair of eyes.
  >  18:
  >  19:**Core principle:** The plan already did the thinking. Execute it exactly,
  >  20:prove each step with a test you watched fail and then pass, and leave a
  >  21:record that survives your own forgetting.
  >  22:
  >  23:**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
  >  24:ledger and the tool results carry the record.
  >  25:
  >  26:**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner
  >  27:between tasks. They chose inline execution to spend less, not to answer
  >  28:"should I continue?" after every task. Execute all tasks from the plan
  >  29:without stopping.

  > 115:loses its place re-implements tasks whose commits already exist — the same
  > 116:failure as a controller re-dispatching them, paid for in your own context.
  > 117:Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. Harness todos are a
  > 118:live view; the ledger is the record.
  > 119:
  > 120:The workspace and ledger are shared with superpowers:subagent-driven-development
  > 121:— same directory, same format — so a plan can change executors mid-flight
  > 122:and the new one resumes from the same ledger.
  > 123:
  > 124:- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run
  > 125:  `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it
  > 126:  prints the plan's git-ignored directory
  > 127:  (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to every
  > 128:  artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, review packages. Another plan's
  > 129:  directory is never yours to read or write.
  > 130:- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  > 131:  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
  > 132:  DONE — do not redo them; resume at the first task without one. Their
  > 133:  commits exist in git even when your context no longer remembers making
  > 134:  them: after compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own
  > 135:  recollection. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file is
  > 136:  another plan's progress: leave it and start your own, fresh.
  > 137:- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  > 138:  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
  > 139:- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch);
  > 140:  if that happens, recover from `git log`.
  > 141:
  > 142:Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
  > 143:todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
  > 144:authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
  > 145:against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
  > 146:rulings made without one are provisional.
  > 147:
  > 148:**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** load superpowers:test-driven-development now,
  > 149:before Task 1. It governs every step of every task below; a plan whose
  > 150:steps already say "write the failing test first" does not exempt you
  > 151:from reading it.
  > 152:
  > 153:Before Task 1, scan the plan for conflicts between tasks. The plan's
  > 154:Interfaces blocks tell you where to look: for every task that consumes
  > 155:what an earlier task produces, one ledger row — the two tasks, what one
  > 156:produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. Tasks that
  > 157:share nothing get no row; a plan whose tasks share nothing gets the single
  > 158:line `Pre-flight: no shared interfaces`. Rule on each conflict a row
  > 159:surfaces with the spec as the binding authority, record the ruling beside
  > 160:its row, and start Task 1. Each task's own text is checked when you read
  > 161:its brief, not here.
  > 162:
  > 163:## The Task Loop
  > 164:
  > 165:Everything you print, and every tool result, stays resident in your
  > 166:context for the rest of the session. Redirect long test output to a file
  > 167:in the workspace and read its tail; read a brief, not the whole plan.
  > 168:
  > 169:### 1. Take the task
  > 170:
  > 171:- Run this skill's `scripts/task-start PLAN_FILE N`. It prints the brief
  > 172:  path and BASE (the commit the task's range is cut from) in one call.
  > 173:  Read the brief for every task, including ones you remember from setup:
  > 174:  what you remember is a summary, the brief has the exact values,
  > 175:  signatures, and test cases.
  > 176:- Mark the task's todo in_progress.
  > 177:
  > 178:Every tool call is a turn that re-reads your whole context. Bookkeeping
  > 179:rides along with work — a ledger append in the same call as the commit,
  > 180:never in a call of its own.
  > 181:
  > 182:### 2. Work the steps
  > 183:
  > 184:The plan's steps are already in RED-GREEN order; follow them in that
  > 185:order under superpowers:test-driven-development, loaded at setup. A test
  > 186:step's code is written first and run first. Watching it fail is a step,
  > 187:not a formality — a test that passes before the implementation exists is
  > 188:a finding about the test.
  > 189:
  > 190:Every step that runs a command has an `Expected:` line. Run the command,
  > 191:read its output, and compare. Three outcomes:
  > 192:
  > 193:- **Matches.** Next step.
  > 194:- **The code is wrong.** Use superpowers:systematic-debugging. Find the
  > 195:  cause; never patch the symptom to make the step's output match.
  > 196:- **The plan is wrong** — a step contradicts the spec, an interface from an
  > 197:  earlier task doesn't match what this task consumes, a command that
  > 198:  cannot work. Rule on the smallest change that satisfies the spec, ledger
  > 199:  it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`, and
  > 200:  continue. The ruling is carried, not remembered: later tasks that touch
  > 201:  the same interface read it from the ledger.
  > 202:
  > 203:Commit as the plan's commit steps say. A task that spans several commits
  > 204:is fine; BASE is what the review range is cut from, never `HEAD~1`.
  > 205:
  > 206:### 3. The completion contract
  > 207:
  > 208:Before a task's ledger line, all of the following are true, with evidence
  > 209:in this session — not inferred from the diff looking right:
  > 210:
  > 211:- Every test the brief names exists and ran in this task, and you read
  > 212:  the output.
  > 213:- The final test run for the task passed — `task-done` is that run, and
  > 214:  it writes the command and result into the ledger line.
  > 215:- Every `Expected:` line in the brief was compared against real output.
  > 216:- Every deviation from the brief has a `Ruling:` line in the ledger.
  > 217:
  > 218:**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** superpowers:verification-before-completion governs
  > 219:the claim. If any item is missing, the task is not complete: finish it.
  > 220:
  > 221:### 4. Complete the task
  > 222:
  > 223:Run this skill's `scripts/task-done PLAN_FILE N BASE -- <test command>`
  > 224:with the test command the brief names for the whole task. It runs the
  > 225:tests, keeps the full output in the workspace, prints the tail, and — only
  > 226:if they pass — appends the completion line to the ledger:
  > 227:
  > 228:`Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, tests: <command> → <result>)`
  > 229:
  > 230:A failing run records nothing; the task is not complete. When it records,
  > 231:mark the todo complete and take the next task.
  > 232:
  > 233:## Final Review
  > 234:
  > 235:Run `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`
  > 236:(MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g.
  > 237:`git merge-base main HEAD`) and review from the file it prints.
  > 238:
  > 239:**With a subagent tool:** dispatch the reviewer on the most capable
  > 240:available model — the whole-branch review is a judgment task — using
  > 241:superpowers:requesting-code-review's
  > 242:[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md), with the
  > 243:package path, the plan and spec paths, the plan's Review Focus section
  > 244:verbatim if it has one (the input classes and failure modes the plan's
  > 245:tests do not exercise — the reviewer checks each deliberately), and a
  > 246:pointer to the ledger's `Ruling:` lines so it can weigh the calls you
  > 247:made. Specify the model
  > 248:explicitly; an omitted model inherits the session's, which may not be the
  > 249:most capable. This is the one fresh context the whole run buys. Do not
  > 250:skip it, and do not replace it with your own read of the diff.
  > 251:
  > 252:**Without a subagent tool:** read code-reviewer.md and perform that review
  > 253:yourself against the package, as a separate pass after the last task's
  > 254:ledger line. Write `Final review: self-review (no subagent tool)` to the
  > 255:ledger, and say so in your final message: a self-review by the author is
  > 256:weaker than a fresh reviewer, and your human partner decides whether that
  > 257:is enough before merge.
  > 258:
  > 259:Sort the findings before you act on any of them. The reviewer's severity
  > 260:labels are advice; the gate is yours. Its "Declined to judge" list is
  > 261:yours too: every line there is a ruling you make and ledger, exactly like
  > 262:a plan conflict — `Final: Ruling: <behavior the reviewer set aside> —
  > 263:<what a reasonable person using this software gets, and why that stands
  > 264:or why it is now a finding> — <cost if wrong>`. Re-grade first, by effect: the
  > 265:spec is a vision document, and a finding's grade is what a reasonable
  > 266:person using this software gets if it ships, not whether the spec names
  > 267:the input that triggers it — a reviewer who set a finding at Minor
  > 268:because the spec was silent has graded the spec, not the effect. Then:
  > 269:
  > 270:- **Critical and Important** enter the fix pass.
  > 271:- **Minor** goes to the ledger as `Final: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`
  > 272:  and to your final message under "Deferred minors". Minors never enter
  > 273:  the fix pass, and never become rulings — a ruling is a decision about a
  > 274:  conflict, not a note that you declined a polish suggestion.
  > 275:
  > 276:Fix the Critical and Important findings yourself — you are the
  > 277:implementer here — in ONE pass. Each fix is verified by TDD, not by a
  > 278:second reviewer: write the test that reproduces the finding, watch it
  > 279:fail, make it pass, then run the whole suite. Record each in the ledger as
  > 280:`Final: fixed <finding> — <test name> RED→GREEN, suite <N>/<N>`. A fix
  > 281:without a test that failed first is not verified; a suite that is not
  > 282:green after the pass means the pass is not over. Do not dispatch a
  > 283:re-review: it would re-read a diff whose covering tests already answer
  > 284:"addressed" and whose suite run already answers "broke nothing".
  > 285:
  > 286:A finding you decide not to fix is a ruling — `Final: Ruling: <finding> —
  > 287:<why the code stands> — <cost if wrong>` — and reaches your human partner
  > 288:in the rulings list. There is no second fix pass.
  > 289:
  > 290:## Finish
  > 291:
  > 292:Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing
  > 293:`Ruling:` into your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you
  > 294:made them, each with what it costs if wrong, and every `minor (deferred)`
  > 295:line under "Deferred minors". Both lists are exhaustive. Your final
  > 296:message is the only place the decisions you took on your human partner's
  > 297:behalf — and the findings you chose not to act on — reach them.
  > 298:
  > 299:When the final review is clean and its fixes are committed, delete this
  > 300:plan's workspace directory — the git history is the record now. Sibling
  > 301:directories belong to other plans; leave them alone.
  > 302:
  > 303:Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
  > 304:
  > 305:## Common Rationalizations
  > 306:
  > 307:| Excuse | Reality |
  > 308:|--------|---------|
  > 309:| "I remember what Task N says" | You remember a summary. The brief has the exact values. Read it. |
  > 310:| "The plan's code is right, skip watching the test fail" | A test you never saw fail proves nothing. It is one step. Run it. |
  > 311:| "I'll run the full suite at the end instead of per step" | Per-step runs are how you learn which step broke it. The end-of-task run is the contract, not a substitute. |
  > 312:| "The plan is wrong here, I'll just do the right thing" | Do the right thing and ledger the ruling. Unledgered deviation is a decision made in secret. |
  > 313:| "I'll write the ledger lines after a few tasks" | Compaction does not wait for a convenient moment. One line per task, in the same message as the commit. |
  > 314:| "Let me check in before the next task" | They chose inline to spend less. Progress prompts spend their time instead. Only the four stops stop you. |
  > 315:| "I read my own diff carefully; the final reviewer is redundant" | Same author, same blind spots. The reviewer is the only fresh context this run buys. |
  > 316:| "Tests should pass, the change was trivial" | "Should" is not evidence. The contract requires the command and its output. |
  > 317:| "Subagents are slow and expensive, I'll skip the final review too" | Inline already removed the per-task reviewers. One review of the whole branch is the floor, not the ceiling. |
  > 318:| "The reviewer said Minor, so it's Minor" | The label graded the spec's silence. Grade what the person gets. Re-grade, then gate. |
  > 319:| "The fix is obvious, no need for a failing test first" | The failing test is the only proof the finding was real and is now gone. Without it you have a diff and a hope. |
  > 320:| "I'll fix the minors too while I'm in there" | Every minor you fix is a test, a fix, and a suite run your partner did not ask for. Ledger them; your partner decides. |"]}
